title: Group, summarize, and compare
goal: Distinguish group summaries, row-aligned transformations, and group filters.
prerequisites: You can select columns, use summary methods, and create new columns.

cells.title: One question for each group
cells.explanation: `groupby()` splits rows according to a label, then a summary method calculates one result per group. Named aggregation lets you choose readable output names. Here each campus receives its own row count and mean score.
cells.code:
df = students()
result = df.groupby("Campus", as_index=False).agg(Students=("Student_ID", "size"), Mean_score=("Score", "mean"))
print(result.round(2))

questions.prompt: What does each row of the result represent?
questions.answer: One campus, with its number of student records and average score.

questions.prompt: How many rows should result contain?
questions.answer: Two, one for Dubai and one for RAK.
It keeps Campus as an ordinary column rather than placing it in the result index.

cells.task: Group by Program instead. Store a DataFrame named result with Program as a normal column and named summary columns Students, Median_score, and Highest_score.
cells.hint: Use named aggregations with size, median, and max.
cells.solution:
df = students()
result = df.groupby("Program", as_index=False).agg(Students=("Student_ID", "size"), Median_score=("Score", "median"), Highest_score=("Score", "max"))
print(result)
cells.solution_note: Both programs have six students. AI has median 88.5 and maximum 95; IT has median 74.0 and maximum 82.

check.prompt: How many values does an ordinary mean aggregation return for one group?
options: One value for every original row
check.feedback: An aggregation reduces the group to a summary.

cells.verify:
assert len(result) == 2
assert result["Students"].sum() == 12
assert result.set_index("Campus").loc["RAK", "Students"] == 6
cells.solution_verify:
assert result.set_index("Program").loc["AI", "Median_score"] == 88.5
assert result.set_index("Program").loc["IT", "Highest_score"] == 82
assert result["Students"].sum() == 12
cells.watch: A mean without its supporting count can hide a very small group.
cells.takeaway: Summarize each group with readable labels and counts.

cells.title: Multiple keys and missing group labels
cells.explanation: Grouping by a list of columns forms one group for each observed combination. By default, rows with a missing group key are excluded. `dropna=False` keeps those rows in a separate missing-label group so the totals can be audited.
cells.code:
df = students()
df.loc[0, "Campus"] = None
result = df.groupby(["Campus", "Program"], dropna=False, as_index=False).agg(Students=("Student_ID", "size"), Mean_score=("Score", "mean"))
print(result.round(2))
print("Total represented:", result["Students"].sum())

questions.prompt: What does one result row represent now?
questions.answer: One Campus-Program combination, including a combination whose Campus is missing.

questions.prompt: How many student records are represented in total?
questions.answer: All 12, because dropna=False retains the missing-campus record.

questions.prompt: What would the default dropna=True do to S001?
questions.answer: It would exclude S001 from this grouped result because Campus is missing.

cells.task: Run the same grouping with dropna=True. Compare its represented row total with len(df), and store the grouped table in result.
cells.hint: Keep the original table; add the group sizes and compare the sum.
cells.solution:
df = students()
df.loc[0, "Campus"] = None
result = df.groupby(["Campus", "Program"], dropna=True, as_index=False).agg(Students=("Student_ID", "size"))
print(result)
print("Represented:", result["Students"].sum(), "Original:", len(df))
cells.solution_note: The grouped counts sum to 11, while the original table still has 12 rows. S001 is excluded only from the grouping output.

check.prompt: Which option retains rows whose grouping key is missing?

cells.watch: When group keys are categorical, set observed explicitly if you need predictable inclusion of unused categories.
cells.takeaway: Reconcile grouped totals with the original table.

cells.title: A summary for every original row
cells.explanation: `transform()` returns values aligned with the original rows. A group mean can therefore be attached to every student in that group. This makes comparisons with a group benchmark possible without reducing the table to one row per group.
cells.code:
df = students()
df["Program_mean"] = df.groupby("Program")["Score"].transform("mean")
df["Difference"] = df["Score"] - df["Program_mean"]
result = df[["Student_ID", "Program", "Score", "Program_mean", "Difference"]]
print(result.round(2))

questions.prompt: How many rows does result keep?
Will all AI students have the same Program_mean?
questions.answer: Yes. The same AI group mean is aligned with each AI student.

questions.prompt: Why would assigning a two-row group mean Series directly be risky?
questions.answer: Pandas aligns by index labels, which may not match the original row index. transform is designed to return a row-aligned result.

cells.task: Calculate the median score within each campus in a column named Campus_median. Keep only students scoring strictly above that median. Store Student_ID, Campus, Score, and Campus_median in result.
cells.solution:
df = students()
df["Campus_median"] = df.groupby("Campus")["Score"].transform("median")
result = df.loc[df["Score"] > df["Campus_median"], ["Student_ID", "Campus", "Score", "Campus_median"]]
print(result)
cells.solution_note: Six students are above their campus median: S001, S003, S006, S007, S010, and S012.

check.prompt: Which operation returns a group statistic aligned to every original row?
check.feedback: transform preserves the original row alignment while applying group-specific calculations.

cells.watch: A group-relative label and a fixed-threshold label answer different questions.
cells.takeaway: Use transform when the result belongs beside the original records.

cells.title: Keep whole groups and control unused categories
cells.explanation: A group filter keeps or removes whole groups based on a group-level rule. Categorical columns can also contain labels with no rows. `observed=True` limits a group result to categories actually present in the data.
cells.code:
df = students()
df["Program"] = pd.Categorical(df["Program"], categories=["AI", "IT", "CS"])
result = df.groupby("Program", observed=True)["Score"].agg(["size", "mean"])
print(result.round(2))

questions.prompt: Does declaring CS as a category create CS student records?
questions.answer: No. It declares a possible label without adding rows.

questions.prompt: Will CS appear in this grouped result?
questions.answer: No, because observed=True reports only categories that occur in the data.

questions.prompt: How is filtering whole groups different from filtering scores >= 80?
questions.answer: A group filter keeps all rows in an accepted group, including individual scores below 80.

cells.task: Start from students(). Keep all students in programs whose mean Score is at least 80 using groupby().filter().
cells.hint: The filter function receives each group DataFrame; compare its Score mean with 80.
cells.solution:
df = students()
result = df.groupby("Program").filter(lambda group: group["Score"].mean() >= 80)
print(result[["Student_ID", "Program", "Score"]])
cells.solution_note: All six AI students remain, including S011 with score 68. The rule concerns the program mean, not each individual score.

check.prompt: A program passes the group-mean rule. Which records are kept by groupby().filter()?
check.feedback: A group filter accepts or rejects the group as a whole.

cells.watch: Unused categories and missing labels are different: observed controls unused categories; dropna controls missing keys.
cells.takeaway: Separate group inclusion rules from row inclusion rules.
